newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland's Kwasniewski hails Clinton's new term.
newsitem.headline: Poland's Kwasniewski hails Clinton's new term.

text.p: Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski said on Wednesday that Bill Clinton's re-election would give the U.S. leader's presidency a new historic dimension and praised his support for NATO enlargement.
"As a result of your second election victory your mission has taken on a new historic dimension," Kwasniewski wrote to Clinton.

"All in Poland highly value your consistent involvement in the process of enlarging NATO," Kwasniewski added, lauding Clinton's campaign pledge in Detroit last month that the Western defence alliance should be enlarged by 1999.

Rapid NATO entry is a top priority shared by all main parties in Poland, which threw off Soviet domination in 1989 and is now widely acknowledged to be in the first wave of future NATO members along with Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Polish politicians said there had been little difference between Clinton and Republican Bob Dole on this key issue.

"We have been observing these elections fairly calmly for some time, as both candidates spoke clearly for enlarging NATO by 1999 -- Dole even gave an earlier date (of 1998)," senior opposition parliamentarian Janusz Onyszkiewicz told Reuters.

He said the central question was how many supporters of enlargement had been returned to the Senate, which will have to ratify the necessary change in the Washington Treaty with a two-thirds majority -- 67 out of the 100 votes.
Some U.S. politicians question NATO's enlargement, out of reluctance to extend guarantees to distant states or to harm relations with Russia,which opposes Poland's membership.
But up to 10 million U.S. voters of Polish origin give politicians a reason to back the country's aspirations.

The deputy parliamentary head of Poland's ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), Longin Pastusiak, said Clinton was good for Poland and he hoped the president would increase U.S. financial help for future members' costly efforts to bring their armed forces in line with NATO standards.
"If he did that, then one could say he had fulfilled all of Poland's expectations," Pastusiak told PAP news agency.
